Test-retest reliability of each threshold, from your own repeated tests

Source: R/compare.R
lactate_reliability.Rd

The typical error of each threshold, from athletes who did the same test two or more times while their fitness did not change (e.g. a few days apart): the residual standard deviation of a two-way analysis of athletes and tests, which leaves out the mean change from one test to the next (Hopkins, 2000). It is given in intensity units and as a coefficient of variation, 100 * (exp(s) - 1), with s the typical error of the log intensities. Pass the result to compare_tests(cv = ) so that its verdicts use the noise of your own protocol, analyzer and athletes rather than the default values, from trained male cyclists.

Usage

lactate_reliability(x, athlete, test)

Arguments

x

The result of lactate_threshold() with .by, one group per athlete and test (e.g. .by = c("athlete", "test")).

athlete, test

The columns of x that name the athlete and the test (e.g. the test number or date). Tests are matched by their order within each athlete: first, second, and so on.

Value

a tibble with one row per method: method, n_athletes (with two or more tests), n_tests, bias (the mean change from one test to the next, intensity units), typical_error (intensity units), cv (%) with its 90% confidence interval (cv_low, cv_high), and the degrees of freedom of the typical error (df). Methods with fewer than two such athletes get NA.

Details

A typical error from few athletes is itself uncertain: with 10 athletes and 2 tests (9 degrees of freedom) its 90% confidence interval spans 0.73 to 1.65 times its value (from the chi-square distribution of a variance). The result therefore gives the degrees of freedom (df) and that interval for the cv (cv_low, cv_high), as reliability statistics should always come with one (Sainani, 2017), and compare_tests() widens its intervals for a small df. Atkinson & Nevill (1998) recommend more than 40 athletes for a reliability study; with fewer, read the interval.

The bias is the mean change from each test to the next, which the typical error leaves out. Report it beside the random error (Atkinson & Nevill, 1998): a bias that is not near zero is a learning or order effect, or a change in fitness between the tests. The cv assumes that the error grows with the intensity, as it usually does for such measures; with athletes of a similar level the two cannot be told apart, and typical_error is the same noise in intensity units.

References

Atkinson G, Nevill AM. Statistical methods for assessing measurement error (reliability) in variables relevant to sports medicine. Sports Medicine. 1998;26(4):217-238.

Hopkins WG. Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Medicine. 2000;30(1):1-15.

Sainani KL. Reliability statistics. PM&R. 2017;9(6):622-628. doi:10.1016/j.pmrj.2017.05.001

Examples

## the same athlete tested twice, a few days apart (simulated here as small changes in lactate)
set.seed(1)
repeats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(a) do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(t) {
  transform(demo_data, athlete = a, test = t, intensity = intensity * (0.9 + 0.05 * a),
            lactate = lactate * exp(rnorm(nrow(demo_data), 0, 0.05)))
}))))
results <- lactate_threshold(repeats, intensity, lactate, method = c("OBLA", "Dmax"), plot = FALSE,
                             .by = c("athlete", "test"))
reliability <- lactate_reliability(results, "athlete", "test")
reliability
